newsitem.title: USA: G7 sees faster economic growth, pledges to aid poor.
newsitem.headline: G7 sees faster economic growth, pledges to aid poor.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
The Group of Seven richest industrial nations on Saturday forecast better times ahead for the world economy and pledged to help poor nations benefit from the coming prosperity.
After a six-hour meeting that seemed remarkably short of rancour, top finance officials from the group also voiced broad satisfaction with the recent stability of currency rates.
"Conditions appear to be in place for a strengthening and broadening of the expansion of the world economy into 1997," U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told reporters.
Inflation is low, trade is in better balance and government budget deficits are being reduced, he said.

With the outlook for the world -- and their own -- economies -- brightening and currencies stable, officials from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States were able to concentrate on helping the less well off.
As a part of a multilateral debt relief initiative, the G7 pledged to sharply expand its aid for poor countries saddled with too many foreign loans.
Rubin said the G7 and other creditor countries are now prepared to write off up to 80 percent of their loans to eligible poor nations, up from 67 percent before.

That should pave the way for the formal launch of the multilateral debt relief plan during the current annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank that winds up on October 3. The G7 gathering took place on the fringes of that meeting.

"I hope we will be able to have the first countries to benefit from (the debt initiative)...before the end of the year," Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said. Uganda is expected to be among those.

The relative tranquility of the world economy also allowed the G7 finance ministers and central banks to concentrate on longer-term issues, particularly Europe's plan to launch a single currency in 1999.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the G7 wants to make sure that the new European currency is as stable and as secure as the German mark. The mark and the currencies of the other countries participating in European Monetary Union will be replaced by the "euro" on Jan. 1, 1999.

"When the mark disappears, its successor currency should be able to take exactly the role of the mark," the head of the German central bank said, noting that the German currency is the world's second most important after the U.S. dollar.

If that does not happen, global investors might shift massive amounts of funds into dollars, disrupting currency markets and distorting worldwide trade. "No one is interested in that happening," Tietmeyer said.

For the moment, though, the G7 is mainly interested in keeping the dollar strong, officials from various countries said. By keeping down the price of U.S. imports, a strong dollar helps keep a lid on American inflation at a time when the economy here is steaming ahead.
At the same time, the strong dollar benefits Europe and Japan, at a time when their economies are struggling, by making their exports more competitive on world markets.

In the run-up to the meeting, U.S. officials had stressed the importance of both Europe and Japan nurturing their fledgling economic recoveries. Rubin apparently came away from Saturday's gathering satisfied on that score.

"Japan's economy is continuing gradual growth," Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita told reporters. "Our monetary policy will emphasise putting the basis for the current economic recovery on firmer ground."
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said his country's economy was also on the uspwing.

Some analysts have voiced concern that Europe's head-long drive to meet the tough conditions set out for the launch of the euro in 1999 will undercut the continent's fledgling upswing and have called for an easing of the criteria.
But Waigel said that was not the G7's view.
He told reporters that the group in general had agreed that the strict economic conditions laid down for the start of the European Monetary Union should not be weakened.
"The G7 supported a strict adherence to the criteria," he said.
